summary: Defines CHAP, a way for one side of a PPP link to check the identity of the other. The checker sends a random challenge, and the peer replies with a hash computed from the challenge and a shared secret, so the secret itself is never sent.

plainLanguage.summary: CHAP lets one end of a PPP link check that the other end knows a shared secret. The peer proves this by answering a changing challenge, so it does not send the secret itself.

questions: what is the chap packet format
subtitle: How a PPP link checks a peer with a changing challenge instead of sending its secret.

tldr.problem: A point-to-point link may need to verify the identity of the peer before network-layer traffic is allowed. Sending the shared secret across the link would expose it.
tldr.mechanism: The authenticator sends a changing challenge. The peer returns a one-way hash of the identifier, secret, and challenge, and the authenticator checks the result.
tldr.outcome: The secret is not sent over the link, but both ends must hold it in plaintext form. RFC 1994 obsoletes RFC 1334 and is updated by RFC 2484.

today: RFC 1994 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1334 and is updated by RFC 2484. Its procedures describe CHAP authentication on PPP links.

sections.title: Authentication During PPP Setup
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) first establishes a data link. It can then run an optional Authentication phase before network-layer protocols transmit over that link. Authentication is not required by default; an implementation that wants it MUST specify an Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option during Link Establishment.

The end that requires authentication is the authenticator. The other end, whose identity is checked, is the peer. The RFC mainly describes links between hosts or routers and a PPP network server, including switched circuits and dial-up links.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP can check a peer after establishing the link and before network traffic starts. The check is optional unless the implementation requests an authentication protocol during setup.

sections.title: The Challenge and Response
sections.content:
The Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP) uses a three-way exchange to verify the peer. The authenticator sends a challenge, the peer returns a value computed with a one-way hash, and the authenticator compares that value with its own calculation. If they match, authentication succeeds; otherwise the connection SHOULD be terminated.

The response hash is calculated from the one-octet Identifier, followed by the shared secret, followed by the Challenge Value. The secret is known to both ends and is never sent over the link. The authenticator can send a new challenge at random intervals after setup.
sections.plainLanguage: The authenticator sends a fresh challenge, and the peer combines it with the shared secret to calculate a reply. The authenticator performs the same calculation and checks whether the values match.

sections.title: What CHAP Protects and Requires
sections.content:
An incrementally changing Identifier and a variable challenge help protect against playback of an old response. Challenges should be unique and unpredictable, and repeated challenges limit the time that any one attack can be useful. Negotiating CHAP in both directions can provide mutual authentication.

CHAP requires the secret to be available in plaintext form at both ends, so irreversibly encrypted password databases cannot be used. The secret MUST be at least one octet and SHOULD be large and hard to guess; the RFC prefers a secret at least as long as the hash value used.

CHAP cannot protect against real-time active wiretapping. The RFC also warns against using the same secret in both directions and recommends associating each user name with exactly one authentication method, to avoid forcing use of a weaker method.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing challenges make old answers harder to reuse, but each end still needs access to the actual secret. CHAP cannot stop real-time wiretapping, and the RFC warns against reusing one secret in both directions.

sections.title: Configuration and Packet Fields
sections.content:
PPP negotiates CHAP with an Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option whose Type is 3, Length is 5, and protocol value is c223 in hexadecimal. The Algorithm field is one octet; algorithm 5, CHAP with MD5, is required to be implemented.

Each CHAP packet has a one-octet Code, a one-octet Identifier, a two-octet Length, and Data. The four codes are Challenge (1), Response (2), Success (3), and Failure (4). Challenge and Response data contain a Value-Size, a Value, and a Name; Success and Failure carry a human-readable message that MUST NOT affect protocol operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A CHAP packet identifies its type, links the reply to a challenge, and states the packet length. The type tells the receiver whether the packet carries a challenge, response, success, or failure.

sections.title: Matching Replies and Handling Failure
sections.content:
The authenticator changes both the Identifier and Challenge Value every time it sends a Challenge. The Response copies the challenge's Identifier, allowing the authenticator to match the answer to the current request. The authenticator sends additional challenges until it receives a valid response or an optional retry counter expires.

If the response value matches, the authenticator MUST send Success. If it does not match, the authenticator MUST send Failure and SHOULD take action to terminate the link. The authenticator must also allow repeated Responses during the Network-Layer Protocol phase because a Success may have been lost; a repeated response for the current Identifier receives the same reply code.
sections.plainLanguage: The Identifier connects each response to the challenge it answers, and each new challenge has a new Identifier. A matching hash gets Success; a mismatch gets Failure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The secret SHOULD NOT be the same in both directions. Otherwise an attacker could replay a peer's challenge and use the resulting response to authenticate in the other direction.

The RFC says that assigning multiple authentication methods to one user name can expose the user to negotiation down to a less secure method, such as PAP. It recommends identifying exactly one method for each user name and limiting access to stored secrets and to the systems that distribute them.
sections.plainLanguage: Use separate secrets in the two directions and do not let one user name fall back to a weaker authentication method. Store and distribute secrets so as few parties as possible can access them.

messages.label: Success or Failure
messages.note: Reports whether the calculated values matched.
